title: Written Compilation of the Quran
subtitle: How the revelation was set down in ink during the Prophet's own lifetime, then gathered into one verified copy within a year of his death
summary: The Quran was written during Muhammad's lifetime, collected into verified sheets under Abu Bakr, and copied into regional standard codices under Uthman. These were not three different Qurans but stages in preserving one public revelation already memorized and recited by the community.

seo.metaTitle: Written Compilation of the Quran: Abu Bakr, Yamama, and Zayd ibn Thabit
seo.metaDescription: Islamic sources describe a careful written collection under Abu Bakr after the Prophet's death and the production of standard copies under Uthman.

sections.title: The Evidence in Brief
sections.body: Islamic sources describe a written collection under Abu Bakr and standard copies under Uthman. The process did not create revelation. It gathered and standardized material already recited and written by the companions. Early manuscripts support this common text in the first Islamic century.

sections.title: Collection Under Abu Bakr and Uthman
sections.body:
Sahih al-Bukhari 4986 names Zayd ibn Thabit as leader of the first collection after Yamama. The sheets passed from Abu Bakr to Umar and then Hafsa.

Sahih al-Bukhari 4987 describes Uthman's committee copying them during regional disputes. Hafsa was Umar's daughter and a Prophet's widow. The reports are Islamic literary sources, not surviving administrative records. Early manuscripts support the antiquity of the resulting text.

sections.title: From Written Pieces to a Collected Codex
sections.body: Scribes wrote revelation during the Prophet's life. Companions memorized it. After reciters died at Yamama, Abu Bakr commissioned Zayd ibn Thabit to gather the written material. Hafsa kept the sheets. Uthman's committee used them for standard codices (Sahih al-Bukhari 4986–4987).

sections.title: A Different Timescale
sections.body: The Bible's books were composed, copied, and canonized across centuries. The Quran was collected within the first Muslim generation by people who heard its recitation. This does not place every later report beyond examination. It gives the Quran a shorter, more public path to a standard text.

sections.title: Oral and Written Evidence Worked Together
sections.body: The Quran was preserved by memory and writing. Reciters checked written material. Codices constrained recitation. This redundancy supports preservation. An error would have to escape both public recitation and the written record.

sections.title: Compilation Did Not Begin With Uthman
sections.body: Uthman did not gather an unwritten Quran or invent its order. Abu Bakr's collection already existed. Material had been written during Muhammad's life. Uthman produced public codices from that collection as Islam spread.

sections.title: A Traceable Preservation Process
sections.body: Quran 41:42 says falsehood cannot approach the revelation. The process shows practical preservation: scribes, memorization, first-generation collection, custody, and public standardization. The case is cumulative, not one manuscript or narrator.

sections.title: The Central Takeaway
sections.body: The Quran's written history is early and connected. Abu Bakr's sheets and Uthmanic codices are successive preservation stages. They are not competing Qurans.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.body:
Q: Did Muhammad leave one bound copy?
A: No. Revelation continued until his death. The text existed as memorization and separate written pieces.

Q: How many memorizers died at Yamama?
A: Accounts differ. They agree that experienced reciters died, enough to concern Umar and Abu Bakr about relying on memory alone.

Q: Who held the compiled manuscript?
A: Tradition says Abu Bakr, then Umar, then Hafsa bint Umar held it until Uthman used it.

Q: Did compilation change the wording?
A: Muslims hold that it did not. The process gathered and verified written and memorized material.

Q: Was this Uthman's standardization?
A: No. Abu Bakr produced a verified manuscript. Uthman later used it for standard copies and regional disputes.

sections.title: Further Reading
sections.body:
Selected sources and further reading:

- **The History of the Qur'anic Text from Revelation to Compilation** — M. M. Al-Azami. Study of Quran compilation.
- **Qur'ans of the Umayyads** — François Déroche. Study of early Quran manuscripts.
- **Misquoting Jesus** — Bart D. Ehrman. Study of New Testament transmission.
- **The Text of the New Testament: Its Transmission, Corruption, and Restoration** — Bruce M. Metzger. Textbook on New Testament manuscripts.

faq.question: Did Muhammad leave behind one single bound copy of the whole Quran?
faq.answer: No. Because revelation continued until his death, the text existed during his lifetime as memorized recitation plus a body of separate written fragments on different materials, not as one closed book.

faq.question: Exactly how many Quran memorizers died at the Battle of Yamama?
faq.answer: Historical accounts differ on the precise number. What they agree on is that a meaningful number of experienced reciters were among the dead, enough to seriously worry Umar and Abu Bakr about the risk of losing material if the community continued to rely on memory alone.

faq.question: Who held the finished compiled manuscript?
faq.answer: According to the traditional account, it remained with Abu Bakr, then passed to Umar during his caliphate, and afterward to Hafsa bint Umar, one of the Prophet's widows, until it was drawn on again under Uthman roughly two decades later.

faq.question: Does calling this a 'compilation' mean the wording changed after Muhammad's death?
faq.answer: Muslims hold that it did not. The process was about gathering and verifying material that already existed in both written and memorized form, not adding, removing, or rewording content.

faq.question: Is this the same event as the Uthmanic standardization?
faq.answer: No. Abu Bakr's compilation produced one complete, verified manuscript shortly after the Prophet's death. Uthman's later project, roughly two decades on, used that same base text to produce standardized copies for a rapidly growing empire and to settle regional recitation disputes - a distinct, later stage covered in a separate article.

furtherReading.title: The History of the Qur'anic Text from Revelation to Compilation
furtherReading.author: M. M. Al-Azami
furtherReading.note: A detailed study by a Muslim scholar of the compilation process under Abu Bakr and Zayd ibn Thabit's role in it, compared with the transmission history of the Bible.

furtherReading.title: Qur'ans of the Umayyads
furtherReading.author: François Déroche
furtherReading.note: An academic study of early Quran manuscripts by a leading Western scholar of Quranic paleography.

furtherReading.title: Misquoting Jesus: The Story Behind Who Changed the Bible and Why
furtherReading.author: Bart D. Ehrman
furtherReading.note: A widely read account of New Testament textual transmission by a mainstream biblical scholar, useful for comparing transmission histories.

furtherReading.author: Bruce M. Metzger
furtherReading.note: A classic academic textbook on the manuscript history of the New Testament.
